title: reassembly: Store pointer to first gap
description:
Store pointer to first gap to reduce number of full list traversals
needed when linking new fragments. When all captured fragments are in
order, the first gap is effectively pointing to list tail. The best case
scenario, where the list traversals are completely eliminated, happens
every time for protocols that always have the fragments ordered (most
notably USBLL Full-Speed capture containing Bulk OUT transfers with
a lot of retransmissions).

The memory usage is increased by a single pointer and 32-bit contiguous
length counter per fragment head . The additional CPU usage is constant
per insertion, i.e. does not increase with the number of fragments in
the list.


---

This is alternative approach to !2494 solving the same underlying issue (#17311). This has lower memory impact because the additional memory usage is just in list head and not in the fragments itself (i.e. the fragments are still stored in a singly linked list).

This MR is gives significant speedup for USBLL captures. For example the sample capture from #18625 opens in just 14 seconds instead of 20 minutes 30 seconds.

notes.body: mentioned in merge request !2494

I cannot find any capture file that would trigger the `MERGE_FRAG` call. From the code it seems that it can only be called from PPP or DNP dissectors. Can someone share a capture (can be privately) that hits the `MERGE_FRAG`?
The capture files attached to #12548 and #18644 trigger `MERGE_FRAG` code path.
With this patch a see a significant improvements also with the pcap used in #17311 (load time ~20s)

Can you check it again? Now, the contiguous length is not only used for first gap handling purposes but also in actual reassembly. Note that since !2494 the TCP dissector was changed in a way where the contiguous length might not necessarily be applicable.
Now load time of the same pcap is ~7-8s. Great work!

For things that I tend to analyze, the first gap (which effectively is a tail pointer when all fragments are in order) is all that's really needed. Maybe TCP dissector can already benefit from the first fragment continuous length to save some more list traversals, but I leave that for people who actually work with TCP. Similarly, I also leave traversal between holes for people who actually work with traces that can benefit from it - it should be possible to add on top of this MR, especially that the tricky part (at least to me) was identifying all the places where the list gets modified.

This does not take advantage of first gap as it just starts from head. However, instead of adding elements one by one as done in version 2 and 3 of this MR, it is possible to simply remember both the first added element and if the first added element was **after** or **before** first gap. The actual merging could use the old approach (i.e. keep alternating "source" and "destination" lists on each insertion). Finally, after the lists are merged:
* if first element was added **before** the first gap, invalidate first gap (i.e. `fragment_reset_first_gap()`); OR
* if first element was added **after** the first gap, call `update_first_gap()` with option to force `find_next_gap` to TRUE (e.g. `gboolean multi_insert`)

Looks ok. Tested with a number of various reassembly stress tests and it seems to be fine. Possibly there could be something a little more clever in `fragment_truncate` based on whether the first fragment is before or after the split point instead of always resetting the first gap, but this works fine and I don't know how useful that optimization would be.

There's a few dissectors (the subject of !8844) that always add segments in order and want to quickly get to the end; they could be sped up later thanks to this.

Well, if `prev_fd` was passed to `fragment_reset_first_gap()` (or some wrapper with a name better reflecting what happened), the check would be rather simple. `prev_fd` is NULL if all fragments were removed, so no extra handling in the callers needed.

The inconsistency can be just solved with `fd_head->contiguous_len = MIN(fd_head->contiguous_len, tot_len);` prior to calling `fragment_items_removed`. I'll re-run the full tests with extra sanity checks.
The `fragment_items_removed()` seems to work fine now.
I guess one question is whether merging this is sufficient to close #17311. Arguably yes.
